question: Why and how does the world come to be? (theories of creation listed in Gauḍapāda Kārikā 1.6–1.9)

sides.position: Reported by the text as views of others: prāṇa/puruṣa as source; expansion or production; dream-māyā imagination; the Lord's will; time; enjoyment; sport. The text answers that the fulfilled one (āptakāma) has no longing.

sides.party: unnamed in the text (the Kārikā does not say whose view this is)
sides.position: Creation is the mere will of the Lord (1.8); or for enjoyment (1.9); or for sport (1.9); or a manifestation/production (1.7); or from time (1.8); or prāṇa/puruṣa (1.6). Each is stated as the view of some group.

notes: Recorded as stated; positions are the text's report of others' views, not the extractor's attributions.

question: What is the world made of? (specialists' views recorded in Gauḍapāda Kārikā 2.20–2.28)

sides.position: Each specialist says the thing is what he knows: prāṇa, beings, guṇas, principles (tattvas), quarters, objects, worlds, gods, Vedas, sacrifices, enjoyer/enjoyed, subtle/gross, time, direction, mind, intellect, thought, creation, dissolution, continuance; principles counted as 25, 26, 31 or endless. The text treats all as imagined (2.30) by the non-separate self (2.19).

sides.party: unnamed in the text (the Kārikā does not say whose view this is)
sides.position: Each specialist takes what he knows (prāṇa, guṇas, tattvas, worlds, etc.) to be the thing; the numbers of principles differ (25, 26, 31, endless).

question: Do the dualists' positions conflict with the non-dual teaching? (Kārikā 3.17–3.18)

sides.position: Dualists, firm in their own doctrines, contradict one another; the non-dual teaching does not contradict them, since duality is said to be the difference (bheda) of the non-dual ultimate.

sides.party: unnamed in the text (the Kārikā does not say whose view this is)
sides.position: The dualists (dvaitin), firm in their own established doctrines, contradict one another (3.17).

question: Is birth of the existent or of the non-existent? (Kārikā 4.3–4.5)

sides.position: Some disputants hold birth of the existent, others (also wise) of the non-existent; the text says neither is born and that each side in refuting the other proclaims non-birth; the author approves that non-birth and does not dispute with them.
arguments: Nothing existent is born; nothing non-existent is born (4.4).

sides.party: unnamed in the text (the Kārikā does not say whose view this is)
sides.position: Birth of the non-existent (abhūta) is held by other disputants; the first group holds birth of the existent (bhūta) (4.3).

question: Can cause and effect be the ground of birth? (Kārikā 4.11–4.23)

sides.position: Against the view that birth arises by cause and effect: if the effect is the cause the cause is born; sequence, simultaneity and mutual dependence each fail; seed-and-sprout equals what is to be proved; inability, non-knowledge and violation of sequence show non-birth.
arguments: Sequence or simultaneity of cause and effect (4.16)

sides.party: unnamed in the text (the Kārikā does not say whose view this is)
sides.position: Birth by cause and effect: the effect is the cause (4.11), or is non-different from it (4.12), or is produced from the born or the unborn (4.13); seed-and-sprout is offered as example (4.20).

notes: The opponent is not named in the text; only the arguments against the position are recorded.
